Open Cup. The club is estimated by <color=#3366CC>Forbes</color> to be the most valuable club in Major League Soccer. The United States
Soccer Federation moved their headquarters from <color=#3366CC>Chicago</color> to Atlanta in 2023 with the help of Falcons and Atlanta
United owner Arthur Blank, with the new training center bearing his name. Atlanta will receive a NWSL team in 2028.
In ice hockey, Atlanta has had two <color=#3366CC>National Hockey League</color> franchises, both of which relocated to a city in Canada
after playing in Atlanta for fewer than 15 years. The Atlanta Flames (now the Calgary Flames) played from 1972 to
1980, and the Atlanta Thrashers (now the Winnipeg Jets) played from 1999 to 2011. The Atlanta Gladiators, a minor
league hockey team in the ECHL, have played in the Atlanta suburb of Duluth since 2003.
The ASUN Conference moved its headquarters to Atlanta in 2019.
Several other emerging sports also have professional franchises in Atlanta. The Georgia Swarm compete in the
<color=#3366CC>National Lacrosse League</color>. The Atlanta Vibe compete in the Pro Volleyball Federation. In Rugby union, on September
21, 2018, Major League Rugby announced that Atlanta was one of the expansion teams joining the league for the 2020
season named Rugby ATL. while in Rugby league, on March 31, 2021, Atlanta Rhinos left the USA Rugby League and
turned fully professional for the first time, joining the new North American Rugby League.
Atlanta has long been known as the "capital" of college football in America. It is home to four-time national champion
Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets football and the Georgia State Panthers. Also, Atlanta is approximately an hour's driving
distance from the eight-time national championship winning Georgia Bulldogs football stadium and within a few hours'
driving distance of many of the other universities that make up the Southeastern Conference, college football's most
profitable and popular conference, and annually hosts the SEC Championship Game. Other annual college football
events include the Aflac Kickoff Game, the Celebration Bowl, the MEAC/SWAC Challenge, and the Chick-fil-A Peach
Bowl which is one of College Football's major New Year's Six Bowl games and a College Football Playoff bowl. Atlanta
additionally hosted the 2018 College Football Playoff National Championship and eventually would the host the 2025
event in the city as well.
Atlanta regularly hosts a variety of sporting events. Most famous was the Centennial 1996 Summer Olympics. The city
has hosted the <color=#3366CC>Super Bowl</color> three times: Super Bowl XXVIII in 1994, Super Bowl XXXIV in 2000, and Super Bowl LIII in
2019. In professional golf, The Tour Championship, the final <color=#3366CC>PGA Tour</color> event of the season, is played annually at East
Lake Golf Club. In 2001 and 2011, Atlanta hosted the <color=#3366CC>PGA Championship</color>, one of the four major championships in
men's professional golf, at the Atlanta Athletic Club. In 2011, Atlanta hosted <color=#3366CC>professional wrestling</color>'s annual
WrestleMania. In soccer, Atlanta has hosted numerous international friendlies and CONCACAF Gold Cup matches.
The city has hosted the NCAA Final Four Men's Basketball Championship five times, most recently in 2020. Atlanta
served as one of the eleven US host cities for the 2026 FIFA World Cup. Every summer, Atlanta hosts the Atlanta
Open, a men's professional tennis tournament.
<color=#3366CC>Running</color> is a popular local sport, and the city declares itself to be "Running City USA". The city hosts the Peachtree
Road Race, the world's largest 10 km race, annually on Independence Day. Atlanta also hosts the nation's largest
Thanksgiving day half marathon, which starts and ends at Center Parc Stadium. The Atlanta Marathon, which starts
and ends at Centennial Olympic Park, routes through many of the city's historic landmarks.
Parks and recreation
Atlanta's 343 parks, nature preserves, and gardens cover 3622 acre, which amounts to only 5.6% of the city's total
acreage, compared to the national average of just over 10%. However, 77% of Atlantans live within a 10-minute walk of
a park, a percentage slightly better than the national average of 76%. In its 2023 ParkScore ranking, The Trust for
Public Land reported that among the park systems of the 100 most populous U.S. cities, Atlanta's park system received
a ranking of 28. Piedmont Park, in Midtown, is Atlanta's most iconic green space. The park, which underwent a major
renovation and expansion in recent years, attracts visitors from across the region and hosts cultural events throughout
the year. Shirley Clarke Franklin Park, a 280-acre green space and reservoir, opened in 2021 and is the city's largest
park. Other notable city parks include Centennial Olympic Park, a legacy of the 1996 Summer Olympics that forms the
centerpiece of the city's tourist district; Woodruff Park, which anchors the campus of Georgia State University; Grant
Park, home to Zoo Atlanta; and Chastain Park, which houses an amphitheater used for live music concerts. The
Chattahoochee River National Recreation Area, in the northwestern corner of the city, preserves a 48 mi stretch of the
river for public recreation opportunities.
The Atlanta Botanical Garden, adjacent to Piedmont Park, contains formal gardens, including a Japanese garden and a
rose garden, woodland areas, and a conservatory that includes indoor exhibits of plants from <color=#3366CC>tropical rainforests</color> and
<color=#3366CC>deserts</color>. The Beltline, a former rail corridor that forms a 22 mi loop around Atlanta's core, has been transformed into a
series of <color=#3366CC>parks</color>, connected by a multi-use trail, increasing Atlanta's park space by 40%.
Atlanta offers resources and opportunities for amateur and participatory sports and recreation. Golf and tennis are
popular in Atlanta, and the city contains six public golf courses and 182 tennis courts. Facilities along the
Chattahoochee River cater to watersports enthusiasts, providing the opportunity for kayaking, canoeing, fishing,
boating, or tubing. The city's only skate park, a 15000 sqft facility that offers bowls, curbs, and smooth-rolling concrete
mounds, is at Historic Fourth Ward Park.
Tree canopy
For a sprawling city with the nation's ninth-largest metro area, Atlanta is surprisingly lush with trees—<color=#3366CC>magnolias</color>,
<color=#3366CC>dogwoods</color>, <color=#3366CC>Southern pines</color>, and magnificent <color=#3366CC>oaks</color>.
Atlanta has a reputation as a "city in a forest" due to an abundance of trees that is rare among major cities. The city's
main street is named after a <color=#3366CC>tree</color>, and beyond the Downtown, Midtown, and Buckhead business districts, the skyline
gives way to a dense canopy of woods that spreads into the suburbs. The city is home to the Atlanta Dogwood Festival,
an annual arts and crafts festival held one weekend during early April, when the native <color=#3366CC>dogwoods</color> are in bloom. The
nickname is factually accurate, as vegetation covers 47.9% of the city as of 2017, the highest among all major
American cities, and well above the national average of 27%. Atlanta's tree coverage does not go unnoticed—it was the
main reason cited by <color=#3366CC>National Geographic</color> in naming Atlanta a "Place of a Lifetime".
The city's lush tree canopy, which filters out pollutants and cools sidewalks and buildings, has increasingly been under
assault from man and nature due to heavy rains, drought, aged forests, new pests, and urban construction. A 2001
study found Atlanta's heavy tree cover declined from 48% in 1974 to 38% in 1996. Community organizations and the
city government are addressing the problem. Trees Atlanta, a non-profit organization founded in 1985, has planted and
distributed over 113,000 shade trees in the city, and Atlanta's government has awarded $130,000 in grants to
neighborhood groups to plant trees. Fees are additionally imposed on developers that remove trees on their property
per a citywide ordinance, active since 1993.
Government
Atlanta is governed by a mayor and the 15-member Atlanta City Council. The city council consists of one member from
each of the city's 12 districts and three at-large members. The mayor may veto a bill passed by the council, but the
council can override the veto with a two-thirds majority. The mayor of Atlanta is Andre Dickens, a Democrat elected on
a nonpartisan ballot whose first term in office began on January 3, 2022. Every mayor elected since 1973 has been
Black. In 2001, Shirley Franklin became the first woman to be elected mayor of Atlanta, and the first African-American
woman to serve as mayor of a major Southern city. Atlanta city politics suffered from a notorious reputation for
corruption during the 1990s administration of Mayor Bill Campbell, who was convicted by a federal jury in 2006 on three
counts of tax evasion in connection with gambling winnings during trips he took with city contractors.
As the state capital, Atlanta is the site of most of Georgia's state government. The Georgia State Capitol building,
located downtown, houses the offices of the governor, lieutenant governor, and secretary of state, as well as the
General Assembly. The Governor's Mansion is in a residential section of Buckhead. Atlanta serves as the regional hub
for many arms of the federal bureaucracy, including the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta and the Centers for Disease
Control and Prevention (CDC). The City of Atlanta annexed the CDC into its territory effective January 1, 2018. Atlanta
also plays an important role in the federal judiciary system, containing the United States Court of Appeals for the
Eleventh Circuit and the United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia.
Historically, Atlanta has been a stronghold for the <color=#3366CC>Democratic Party</color>. Although municipal elections are officially
nonpartisan, nearly all of the city's elected officials are registered Democrats. The city is split among 14 state house
districts and four state senate districts, all held by Democrats. At the federal level, Atlanta is split between three
congressional districts. Most of the city is in the 5th district, represented by Democrat Nikema Williams. Much of
southern Atlanta is in the 13th district, whose seat is currently vacant following the death of Democrat David Scott. A
small portion in the north is in the 11th district, represented by <color=#3366CC>Republican</color> Barry Loudermilk.
Emergency services
The city is served by the Atlanta Police Department (APD), which numbers 2,000 officers and oversaw a 40% decrease
in the city's crime rate between 2001 and 2009. In 2012, <color=#3366CC>Forbes</color> ranked Atlanta as the 6th most dangerous American
city, but by 2023, the city dropped out of its top 10. Despite some improvement in crime, <color=#3366CC>street gangs</color> have continued to
plague the city since the 1980s. In 2022, there was a 200% increase in gang-related charges in the city. In 2023,
Money Inc named Atlanta the third worst gang city in the U.S. Also in 2023, it was estimated that about 1,000 gangs in
the Atlanta area were responsible for at least 70% of all crime including <color=#3366CC>identity theft</color>, credit card fraud, <color=#3366CC>drug trafficking</color>,
and <color=#3366CC>human trafficking</color>. The Georgia Bureau of Investigation Gang Task Force in partnership with the APD is leading
efforts in dismantling gang activity and arresting culprits.
The Atlanta Fire Rescue Department provides fire protection and first responder emergency medical services to the city
from its 35 fire stations. In 2017, AFRD responded to over 100,000 calls for service over a coverage area of 135.7 mi2.
The department also protects Hartsfield–Jackson with five fire stations on the property, serving over 1 million
passengers from over 100 countries. The department protects over 3000 high-rise buildings, 23 mi of the rapid rail
system, and 60 mi of interstate highway.
The Georgia National Guard is based in the city.
Emergency ambulance services are provided to city residents by hospital-based Grady EMS (Fulton County), and
American Medical Response (DeKalb County).
In January 2017, Atlanta declared itself a "welcoming city" and "will remain open and welcoming to all". Nonetheless,
Atlanta does not consider itself to be a "sanctuary city". Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms said: "Our city does not
support ICE. We don't have a relationship with the U.S. Marshal's Service. We closed our detention center to ICE
detainees, and we would not pick up people on an immigration violation."
In 2025, Atlanta Public Safety Training Center opened a $118 million training center for police and firefighters.
Education
Tertiary education
With more than 15 colleges and universities, including three law schools and two medical schools, Atlanta is
considered one of the nation's largest hubs for <color=#3366CC>higher education</color>. Three universities have earned the highest
classification of "R1: Doctoral Universities – Very high research activity".
The Georgia Institute of Technology, commonly referred to as Georgia Tech, is a prominent public research university
in Midtown. It offers highly ranked degree programs in engineering, design, industrial management, the sciences,
business, and architecture.
Georgia State University is a major public research university based in Downtown Atlanta; it is the second largest in
student population of the 26 public colleges and universities in the University System of Georgia and is a significant
contributor to the revitalization of the city's central business district.
Atlanta is home to nationally renowned private colleges and universities, most notably Emory University, a leading
liberal arts and research institution that operates Emory Healthcare, the largest health care system in Georgia. The City
of Atlanta annexed Emory into its territory effective January 1, 2018.
The Atlanta University Center is also in the city; it is the nation's only contiguous consortium of <color=#3366CC>historically black</color>
<color=#3366CC>colleges</color>, comprising Spelman College, Clark Atlanta University, Morehouse College, and Morehouse School of
Medicine. Atlanta contains a campus of the Savannah College of Art and Design, a private art and design university
that has proven to be a major factor in the recent growth of Atlanta's visual art community. Atlanta also boasts
American Bar Association accredited law schools: Atlanta's John Marshall Law School, Emory University School of
Law, and Georgia State University College of Law.
The University of Georgia's Terry College of Business operates a satellite campus in Atlanta's Buckhead district, a
major financial center in the city. This location facilitates Executive and Professional <color=#3366CC>MBA</color> programs plus executive
education offerings. The Buckhead campus also serves as a hub where Terry students, alumni, faculty, and staff can
engage with the business community.
The Atlanta Regional Council of Higher Education (ARCHE) is dedicated to strengthening synergy among 19 public
and private colleges and universities in the Atlanta region. Participating Atlanta region colleges and universities partner
on joint-degree programs, cross-registration, library services, and cultural events.
Primary and secondary education
Approximately 49,000 students are enrolled in 106 schools in Atlanta Public Schools (APS), some of which are
operated as charter schools. Atlanta is served by many private schools including, without limitation, Atlanta Jewish
Academy, Atlanta International School, The Westminster Schools, Pace Academy, The Lovett School, The Paideia
School, Holy Innocents' Episcopal School and <color=#3366CC>Roman Catholic</color> parochial schools operated by the Archdiocese of
Atlanta.
In 2018, the City of Atlanta annexed a portion of DeKalb County containing the Centers for Disease Control and Emory
University; this portion was to be zoned to the DeKalb County School District until 2024, when it was to transition into
APS. In 2017 the number of children living in the annexed territory who attended public schools was nine.
Media
The primary network-affiliated television stations in Atlanta are WSB-TV 2 (<color=#3366CC>ABC</color>), WAGA-TV 5 (<color=#3366CC>Fox</color>)., WXIA-TV 11
(<color=#3366CC>NBC</color>), WPXA-TV 14 (Ion), WPCH-TV 17, (<color=#3366CC>CW</color>), WUVG-TV 34 (Univision/UniMás), WATL 36 (MyNetworkTV), WANF
46 (Independent), WKTB-CD 47 (Telemundo) and WUPA 69 (<color=#3366CC>CBS</color>). The Atlanta metropolitan area is served by two
public television stations (both <color=#3366CC>PBS</color> member stations) and two public radio stations. WGTV 8 is the flagship station of
the statewide Georgia Public Television network, while WABE-TV 30 is owned by Atlanta Public Schools. Georgia
Public Radio is listener-funded and comprises one <color=#3366CC>NPR</color> member station, WABE, a classical music station also
operated by Atlanta Public Schools. The second public radio, listener-funded <color=#3366CC>NPR</color> member station is WCLK, a jazz
music station owned and operated by Clark Atlanta University.
Atlanta is served by The Atlanta Journal-Constitution, its only major daily newspaper with wide distribution (the AJC
stopped publishing a physical newspaper in 2026 in favor of digital coverage). The Atlanta Journal-Constitution is the
result of a 1950 merger between The Atlanta Journal and The Atlanta Constitution, with staff consolidation occurring in
1982 and separate publication of the morning Constitution and afternoon Journal ceasing in 2001. Alternative weekly
newspapers include Creative Loafing, which has a weekly print circulation of 80,000. Atlanta Daily World is the oldest
Black newspaper in Atlanta and one of the earliest Black newspapers in American history. Atlanta magazine is a
monthly general-interest magazine based in and covering Atlanta.
Transportation
Atlanta's transportation infrastructure comprises a complex network that includes a heavy rail <color=#3366CC>rapid transit</color> system, a
light rail <color=#3366CC>streetcar</color> loop, a multi-county bus system, <color=#3366CC>Amtrak</color> service via the Crescent, multiple freight train lines, an
<color=#3366CC>Interstate Highway System</color>, several airports, including the world's busiest, and over 45 mi of bike paths.
Atlanta has a network of freeways that radiate out from the city, and automobiles are the dominant means of
transportation in the region. Three major <color=#3366CC>interstate highways</color> converge in Atlanta: I-20 (east-west), I-75
(northwest-southeast), and I-85 (northeast-southwest). The latter two combine in the middle of the city to form the
Downtown Connector (I-75/85), which carries more than 340,000 vehicles per day and is one of the most congested
segments of interstate highway in the United States. Atlanta is mostly encircled by Interstate 285, a beltway locally
known as "the Perimeter" that has come to mark the boundary between "Inside the Perimeter" (ITP), the city and
close-in suburbs, and "Outside the Perimeter" (OTP), the outer suburbs and exurbs. The heavy reliance on automobiles
for transportation in Atlanta has resulted in traffic, commute, and air pollution rates that rank among the worst in the
country. The City of Atlanta has a higher than average percentage of households without a car. In 2015, 15.2 percent of
Atlanta households lacked a car, and this percentage increased slightly to 16.4 percent in 2016. The national average
was 8.7 percent in 2016. Atlanta averaged 1.31 cars per household in 2016, compared to a national average of 1.8.
The Metropolitan Atlanta Rapid Transit Authority (MARTA) provides public transportation in the form of buses, heavy
rail, and a downtown light rail loop. Notwithstanding heavy automotive usage in Atlanta, the city's <color=#3366CC>subway</color> system is the
eighth busiest in the country. MARTA rail lines connect key destinations, such as the airport, Downtown, Midtown,
Buckhead, and Perimeter Center. However, significant destinations, such as Emory University and Cumberland, remain
unserved. As a result, a 2011 Brookings Institution study placed Atlanta 91st of 100 metro areas for transit accessibility.
Emory University operates its Cliff shuttle buses with 200,000 boardings per month, while private <color=#3366CC>minibuses</color> supply
Buford Highway. <color=#3366CC>Amtrak</color>, the national rail passenger system, provides service to Atlanta via the Crescent train (New
York–New Orleans), which stops at Peachtree Station. In 2014, the Atlanta Streetcar opened to the public. The
streetcar's line, which is also known as the Downtown Loop, runs 2.7 mi around the downtown tourist areas of
Peachtree Center, Centennial Olympic Park, the Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park, and Sweet Auburn.
The Atlanta Streetcar line is also being expanded on in the coming years to include a wider range of Atlanta's
neighborhoods and important places of interest, with a total of over 50 mi of track in the plan.
<color=#3366CC>Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport</color> is the world's busiest airport as measured by passenger traffic and
aircraft traffic. The facility offers air service to over 150 U.S. destinations and more than 75 international destinations in
50 countries, with over 2,500 arrivals and departures daily. <color=#3366CC>Delta Air Lines</color> maintains its largest hub at the airport.
Situated 10 miles (16 km) south of downtown in Clayton and Fulton counties, the airport covers most of the land inside
a wedge formed by Interstate 75, Interstate 85, and Interstate 285.
Cycling is a growing mode of transportation in Atlanta, more than doubling since 2009, when it comprised 1.1% of all
commutes (up from 0.3% in 2000). Although Atlanta's lack of bike lanes and hilly topography may deter many residents
from cycling, the city's transportation plan calls for the construction of 226 mi of bike lanes by 2020, with the Beltline
helping to achieve this goal. In 2012, Atlanta's first "bike track" was constructed on 10th Street in Midtown. The
two-lane bike track runs from Monroe Drive west to Charles Allen Drive, with connections to the Beltline and Piedmont
Park. Starting in June 2016, Atlanta received a bike sharing program, known as Relay Bike Share, with 100 bikes in
Downtown and Midtown, which expanded to 500 bikes at 65 stations as of April 2017.
According to the 2016 American Community Survey (five-year average), 68.6% of working city of Atlanta residents
commuted by driving alone, 7% carpooled, 10% used public transportation, and 4.6% walked. About 2.1% used all
other forms of transportation, including taxi, bicycle, and motorcycle. About 7.6% worked at home.
The city has also become one of a handful of "scooter capitals", where companies like Lime and Bird have gained a
major foothold by placing electric scooters on street corners and byways.

Antarctica
Antarctica is <color=#3366CC>Earth</color>'s southernmost and least-populated <color=#3366CC>continent</color>. Situated almost entirely south of the <color=#3366CC>Antarctic Circle</color>
and surrounded by the <color=#3366CC>Southern Ocean</color> (also known as the Antarctic Ocean), it contains the geographic <color=#3366CC>South Pole</color>.
Antarctica is the fifth-largest continent, being about 40% larger than <color=#3366CC>Europe</color>, and has an area of 14200000 km2. Most
of Antarctica is covered by the <color=#3366CC>Antarctic ice sheet</color>, with an average thickness of 1.9 km.
Antarctica is, on average, the coldest, driest, and windiest of the continents, and has the highest average <color=#3366CC>elevation</color>. It is
mainly a polar desert, with annual <color=#3366CC>precipitation</color> of over 200 mm along the <color=#3366CC>coast</color> and far less inland. About 70% of the
world's <color=#3366CC>freshwater</color> reserves are frozen in Antarctica, which, if melted, would raise global <color=#3366CC>sea levels</color> by almost 60 m.
Antarctica holds the record for the lowest measured temperature on Earth, 89.2 C. The coastal regions can reach

temperatures over 10 C in the summer. Native species of animals include <color=#3366CC>mites</color>, <color=#3366CC>nematodes</color>, <color=#3366CC>penguins</color>, <color=#3366CC>seals</color> and
<color=#3366CC>tardigrades</color>. Where vegetation occurs, it is mostly in the form of <color=#3366CC>lichen</color> or <color=#3366CC>moss</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>ice shelves of Antarctica</color> were probably first seen in 1820, during a Russian expedition led by <color=#3366CC>Fabian Gottlieb von</color>
<color=#3366CC>Bellingshausen</color> and Mikhail Lazarev. The decades that followed saw further exploration by French, American, and
British expeditions. The first confirmed landing was by a Norwegian team in 1895. In the early 20th century, there were
a few expeditions into the interior of the continent. British explorers <color=#3366CC>Douglas Mawson</color>, Edgeworth David, and Alistair
Mackay were the first to reach the <color=#3366CC>magnetic South Pole</color> in 1909, and the <color=#3366CC>geographic South Pole</color> was first reached in
1911 by <color=#3366CC>Norwegian explorer</color> <color=#3366CC>Roald Amundsen</color>.
Antarctica is <color=#3366CC>governed by about 30 countries</color>, all of which are parties of the 1959 <color=#3366CC>Antarctic Treaty System</color>. According to
the terms of the treaty, military activity, mining, nuclear explosions, and nuclear waste disposal are all prohibited in
Antarctica. Tourism, fishing and research are the main human activities in and around Antarctica. During the summer
months, about 5,000 people reside at research stations, a figure that drops to around 1,000 in the winter. Despite the
continent's remoteness, human activity has a significant effect on it via <color=#3366CC>pollution</color>, <color=#3366CC>ozone depletion</color>, and <color=#3366CC>climate change</color>.
The melting of the potentially unstable West Antarctic ice sheet causes the most uncertainty in century-scale
projections of <color=#3366CC>sea level rise</color>, and the same melting also affects the <color=#3366CC>Southern Ocean overturning circulation</color>, which can
eventually lead to significant impacts on the <color=#3366CC>Southern Hemisphere</color> climate and Southern Ocean productivity.
Etymology
The name given to the continent originates from the word antarctic, which comes from <color=#3366CC>Middle French</color> antartique or
antarctique ('opposite to the <color=#3366CC>Arctic</color>') and, in turn, the <color=#3366CC>Latin</color> antarcticus ('opposite to the north'). Antarcticus is derived
from the <color=#3366CC>Greek</color> - ('anti-') and (arktikos, 'of the Bear, northern'). The Greek philosopher <color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color> wrote in Meteorology
about an "Antarctic region" in c. 350 BC. The Greek geographer Marinus of Tyre reportedly used the name in his world
map from the second century AD, now lost. The <color=#3366CC>Roman</color> authors Gaius Julius Hyginus and <color=#3366CC>Apuleius</color> used for the South
Pole the <color=#3366CC>romanised</color> Greek name polus antarcticus, from which derived the <color=#3366CC>Old French</color> pole antartike (modern pôle
antarctique) attested in 1270, and from there the <color=#3366CC>Middle English</color> pol antartik, found first in a treatise written by the
English author <color=#3366CC>Geoffrey Chaucer</color>.
European ideas regarding the existence of a Terra Australis—a vast continent in the far south of the globe to balance
the northern lands of Europe, Asia, and North Africa—had existed as an intellectual concept since <color=#3366CC>classical antiquity</color>.
Terra Australis was therefore the name used to refer to all hypothetical landmasses proposed to be where Antarctica is
now known to exist. Assertion of the presence of such a land lasted until the European discovery of Australia.
During the early 19th century, explorer <color=#3366CC>Matthew Flinders</color> doubted the existence of a detached continent south of
Australia (then called New Holland) and thus advocated for the "Terra Australis" name to be used for Australia instead.
In 1824, the colonial authorities in <color=#3366CC>Sydney</color> officially renamed the continent of New Holland to Australia, leaving the term
"Terra Australis" unavailable as a reference to Antarctica. Over the following decades, geographers used phrases such
as "the Antarctic Continent". They searched for a more poetic replacement, suggesting names such as Ultima and
Antipodea. Antarctica was adopted in the 1890s, with the first use of the name being attributed to the Scottish
<color=#3366CC>cartographer</color> John George Bartholomew.
Geography
Positioned asymmetrically around the South Pole and largely south of the <color=#3366CC>Antarctic Circle</color> (one of the five major <color=#3366CC>circles</color>
<color=#3366CC>of latitude</color> that mark maps of the world), Antarctica is surrounded by the <color=#3366CC>Southern Ocean</color>. Rivers exist in Antarctica; the
longest is the Onyx. Antarctica covers more than 14.2 e6km2, almost double the area of Australia, making it the
fifth-largest continent, and comparable to the surface area of <color=#3366CC>Pluto</color>. Its coastline is almost 18000 km long: as of 1983, of
the four coastal types, 44% of the coast is floating ice in the form of an <color=#3366CC>ice shelf</color>, 38% consists of ice walls that rest on
rock, 13% is ice streams or the edge of glaciers, and the remaining 5% is exposed rock.
The <color=#3366CC>lakes</color> that lie at the base of the continental <color=#3366CC>ice sheet</color> occur mainly in the McMurdo Dry Valleys or various oases.
<color=#3366CC>Lake Vostok</color>, discovered beneath Russia's Vostok Station, is the largest subglacial lake globally and one of the largest
lakes in the world. It was once believed that the lake had been sealed off for millions of years, but scientists now
estimate its water is replaced by the slow melting and freezing of ice caps every 13,000 years. During the summer, the
ice at the edges of the lakes can melt, and liquid moats temporarily form. Antarctica has both <color=#3366CC>saline</color> and freshwater
lakes.
Antarctica is divided into <color=#3366CC>West Antarctica</color> and <color=#3366CC>East Antarctica</color> by the <color=#3366CC>Transantarctic Mountains</color>, which stretch from
Victoria Land to the <color=#3366CC>Ross Sea</color>. The vast majority of Antarctica is covered by the <color=#3366CC>Antarctic ice sheet</color>, which averages 1.9
km in thickness. The ice sheet extends to all but a few <color=#3366CC>oases</color>, which, with the exception of the McMurdo Dry Valleys,
are located in coastal areas. Several Antarctic ice streams flow to one of the many <color=#3366CC>Antarctic ice shelves</color>, a process
described by <color=#3366CC>ice-sheet dynamics</color>.
East Antarctica comprises Coats Land, <color=#3366CC>Queen Maud Land</color>, Enderby Land, Mac. Robertson Land, Wilkes Land, and
Victoria Land. All but a small portion of the region lies within the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Hemisphere</color>. East Antarctica is largely covered
by the East Antarctic Ice Sheet. There are numerous islands surrounding Antarctica, most of which are volcanic and
very young by geological standards. The most prominent exceptions to this are the islands of the <color=#3366CC>Kerguelen Plateau</color>,
the earliest of which formed around 40 <color=#3366CC>Ma</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Vinson Massif</color>, in the Ellsworth Mountains, is the highest peak in Antarctica at 4892 m. Mount Erebus on Ross Island is
the world's southernmost active <color=#3366CC>volcano</color> and erupts around 10 times each day. Ash from eruptions has been found 300
km from the <color=#3366CC>volcanic crater</color>. There is evidence of a large number of volcanoes under the ice, which could pose a risk to
the ice sheet if activity levels were to rise. The ice dome known as Dome Argus in East Antarctica is the highest
Antarctic ice feature, at 4091 m. It is one of the world's coldest and driest places—temperatures there reach as low as
-90 C, and the annual precipitation is 1 – 3 cm.
Geologic history

From the end of the <color=#3366CC>Neoproterozoic</color> era to the <color=#3366CC>Cretaceous</color>, Antarctica was part of the <color=#3366CC>supercontinent</color> <color=#3366CC>Gondwana</color>.
Modern Antarctica was formed as Gondwana gradually broke apart beginning around 183 Ma. For a large proportion of
the <color=#3366CC>Phanerozoic</color>, Antarctica had a <color=#3366CC>tropical</color> or <color=#3366CC>temperate climate</color>, and it was covered in forests.
Paleozoic era (539–252 Ma)
During the <color=#3366CC>Cambrian period</color>, Gondwana had a mild climate. West Antarctica was partially in the <color=#3366CC>Northern Hemisphere</color>,
and during the time, large amounts of <color=#3366CC>sandstones</color>, <color=#3366CC>limestones</color>, and <color=#3366CC>shales</color> were deposited. East Antarctica was at the

<color=#3366CC>equator</color>, where seafloor <color=#3366CC>invertebrates</color> and <color=#3366CC>trilobites</color> flourished in the tropical seas. By the start of the <color=#3366CC>Devonian period</color>
(416 <color=#3366CC>Ma</color>), Gondwana was in more southern latitudes, and the climate was cooler, though fossils of land plants are
known from then. Sand and <color=#3366CC>silts</color> were laid down in what is now the Ellsworth, Horlick, and Pensacola Mountains.
Antarctica became glaciated during the <color=#3366CC>Late Paleozoic icehouse</color> beginning at the end of the Devonian period (360 Ma),
though glaciation would substantially increase during the late <color=#3366CC>Carboniferous</color>. It drifted closer to the South Pole, and the
climate cooled, though flora remained. After deglaciation during the latter half of the Early <color=#3366CC>Permian</color>, the land became
dominated by glossopterids (an extinct group of seed plants with no close living relatives), most prominently
Glossopteris, a tree interpreted as growing in waterlogged soils, which formed extensive <color=#3366CC>coal</color> deposits. Other plants
found in Antarctica during the Permian include Cordaitales, sphenopsids, ferns, and <color=#3366CC>lycophytes</color>. At the end of the
Permian, the climate became drier and hotter over much of Gondwana, and the glossopterid forest ecosystems
collapsed as part of the <color=#3366CC>Permian–Triassic extinction event</color>. There is no evidence of any <color=#3366CC>tetrapods</color> having lived in
Antarctica during the Paleozoic.
Mesozoic era (252–66 Ma)
The continued warming dried out much of Gondwana. During the <color=#3366CC>Triassic</color> period, Antarctica was dominated by <color=#3366CC>seed</color>
<color=#3366CC>ferns</color> (pteridosperms) belonging to the genus Dicroidium, which grew as trees. Other associated Triassic flora included
ginkgophytes, <color=#3366CC>cycadophytes</color>, <color=#3366CC>conifers</color>, and sphenopsids. <color=#3366CC>Tetrapods</color> first appeared in Antarctica during the Early
Triassic <color=#3366CC>epoch</color>, with the earliest known fossils found in the Fremouw Formation of the Transantarctic Mountains.
<color=#3366CC>Synapsids</color> (also known as "mammal-like reptiles") included species such as <color=#3366CC>Lystrosaurus</color>, and were common during
the Early Triassic.
The <color=#3366CC>Antarctic Peninsula</color> began to form during the <color=#3366CC>Jurassic</color> period (206–146 Ma). Africa separated from Antarctica in the
Jurassic around 160 Ma, followed by the <color=#3366CC>Indian subcontinent</color> in the early Cretaceous (about 125 Ma). Ginkgo trees,
conifers, <color=#3366CC>Bennettitales</color>, <color=#3366CC>horsetails</color>, ferns and cycads were plentiful during the time. About 80 million years ago, flowering
plants became the most diverse groups of plants on the continent. In West Antarctica, coniferous forests dominated
throughout the <color=#3366CC>Cretaceous</color> period (146–66 Ma), though southern beech trees (<color=#3366CC>Nothofagus</color>) became prominent towards
the end of the Cretaceous. <color=#3366CC>Ammonites</color> were common in the seas around Antarctica, and dinosaurs were also present,
though only a few Antarctic dinosaur <color=#3366CC>genera</color> (Cryolophosaurus and Glacialisaurus, from the Early Jurassic Hanson
Formation of the Transantarctic Mountains, and Antarctopelta, Trinisaura, Morrosaurus and Imperobator from Late
Cretaceous of the Antarctic Peninsula) have been described.
Cenozoic era before present (66–10 Ma)
During the early <color=#3366CC>Paleogene</color>, the Antarctic land bridge continued to connect Antarctica with South America as well as to
southeastern Australia. Fauna from the La Meseta Formation in the Antarctic Peninsula, dating to the <color=#3366CC>Eocene</color>, is very
similar to equivalent South American faunas; with <color=#3366CC>marsupials</color>, xenarthrans, <color=#3366CC>litoptern</color>, and astrapotherian <color=#3366CC>ungulates</color>, as
well as gondwanatheres and possibly meridiolestidans. Marsupials are thought to have dispersed into Australia from
South America via Antarctica by the early Eocene.
Around 53 Ma, Australia-<color=#3366CC>New Guinea</color> separated from Antarctica, opening the Tasmanian Passage. The <color=#3366CC>Drake</color>
<color=#3366CC>Passage</color> opened between Antarctica and South America around 30 Ma, resulting in the creation of the Antarctic
Circumpolar Current that completely isolated the continent. Models of Antarctic geography suggest that this current, as
well as a <color=#3366CC>feedback loop</color> caused by lowering <color=#3366CC>CO2</color> levels, caused the creation of small yet permanent polar ice caps. As
CO2 levels declined further the ice began to spread rapidly, replacing the forests that until then had covered Antarctica.
<color=#3366CC>Tundra</color> ecosystems continued to exist on Antarctica until around 14–10 million years ago, when further cooling lead to
their extermination.
Present day
The <color=#3366CC>geology</color> of Antarctica, largely obscured by the continental ice sheet, can be studied via techniques such as <color=#3366CC>remote</color>
<color=#3366CC>sensing</color>, ground-penetrating radar, and satellite imagery. Geologically, West Antarctica closely resembles the South
American <color=#3366CC>Andes</color>. The Antarctic Peninsula was formed by <color=#3366CC>geologic uplift</color> and the transformation of sea bed <color=#3366CC>sediments</color>
into <color=#3366CC>metamorphic rocks</color>.
West Antarctica was formed by the merging of several <color=#3366CC>continental plates</color>, which created a number of mountain ranges
in the region, the most prominent being the Ellsworth Mountains. The presence of the West Antarctic Rift System has
resulted in <color=#3366CC>volcanism</color> along the border between West and East Antarctica, as well as the creation of the Transantarctic
Mountains.
East Antarctica is geologically varied. Its formation began during the <color=#3366CC>Archean</color> Eon (4,000 Ma–2,500 Ma), and stopped
during the Cambrian Period. It is built on a <color=#3366CC>craton</color> of rock, which is the basis of the Precambrian <color=#3366CC>Shield</color>. On top of the
base are coal and sandstones, limestones, and shales that were laid down during the Devonian and Jurassic periods to
form the Transantarctic Mountains. In coastal areas such as the Shackleton Range and Victoria Land, some <color=#3366CC>faulting</color>
has occurred.
Coal was first recorded in Antarctica near the Beardmore Glacier by Frank Wild on the Nimrod Expedition in 1907, and
low-grade coal is known to exist across many parts of the Transantarctic Mountains. The Prince Charles Mountains
contain deposits of <color=#3366CC>iron ore</color>. There are <color=#3366CC>oil</color> and <color=#3366CC>natural gas fields</color> in the Ross Sea.
Climate
Antarctica is the coldest, windiest, and driest of Earth's continents. Near the coast, the temperature can exceed 10 °C
in summer and fall to below 40 °C in winter. Over the elevated inland, it can rise to about 30 °C in summer but fall
below 80 °C in winter.
The lowest natural air temperature ever recorded on Earth was 89.2 C at the Russian Vostok Station in Antarctica on
21 July 1983. A lower air temperature of 94.7 C was recorded in 2010 by satellite—however, it may have been
influenced by ground temperatures and was not recorded at a height of 2 m above the surface as required for official air
temperature records. Antarctica is colder than the <color=#3366CC>Arctic</color> region, as much of Antarctica is over 3000 m above sea level,
where air temperatures are colder. The relative warmth of the <color=#3366CC>Arctic Ocean</color> is transferred through the <color=#3366CC>Arctic sea ice</color> and
moderates temperatures in the Arctic region.
Antarctica is a polar desert with little <color=#3366CC>precipitation</color>; the continent receives an average equivalent to about 150 mm of
water per year, mostly in the form of snow. The interior is drier and receives less than 50 mm per year, whereas the
coastal regions typically receive more than 200 mm. In a few blue-ice areas, the wind and <color=#3366CC>sublimation</color> remove more
snow than is accumulated by precipitation. In the dry valleys, the same effect occurs over a rock base, leading to a
barren and desiccated landscape.
Regional differences
East Antarctica is colder than its western counterpart because of its higher elevation. <color=#3366CC>Weather fronts</color> rarely penetrate
far into the continent, leaving the centre cold and dry, with moderate wind speeds. Heavy snowfalls are common on the
coastal portion of Antarctica, where snowfalls of up to 1.22 m in 48 hours have been recorded. At the continent's edge,
strong <color=#3366CC>katabatic winds</color> off the polar plateau often blow at <color=#3366CC>storm force</color>. During the summer, more <color=#3366CC>solar radiation</color> reaches
the surface at the South Pole than at the <color=#3366CC>equator</color> because of the 24 hours of sunlight received there each day.
Climate change
Ozone depletion
Scientists have studied the <color=#3366CC>ozone layer</color> in the <color=#3366CC>atmosphere</color> above Antarctica since the 1970s. In 1985, British scientists,
working on data they had gathered at Halley Research Station on the Brunt Ice Shelf, discovered a large area of low
<color=#3366CC>ozone</color> concentration over Antarctica. The 'ozone hole' covers almost the whole continent and was at its largest in
September 2006; the longest-lasting event occurred in 2020. The depletion is caused by the <color=#3366CC>emission</color> of
<color=#3366CC>chlorofluorocarbons</color> and halons into the atmosphere, which causes ozone to break down into other gases. The extreme
cold conditions of Antarctica allow <color=#3366CC>polar stratospheric clouds</color> to form. The clouds act as <color=#3366CC>catalysts</color> for chemical
reactions, which eventually lead to the destruction of ozone. The 1987 <color=#3366CC>Montreal Protocol</color> has restricted the emissions
of ozone-depleting substances. The ozone hole above Antarctica is predicted to slowly disappear; by the 2060s, levels
of ozone are expected to have returned to values last recorded in the 1980s.
The ozone depletion can cause a cooling of around 6 C-change in the <color=#3366CC>stratosphere</color>. The cooling strengthens the <color=#3366CC>polar</color>
<color=#3366CC>vortex</color> and so prevents the outflow of the cold air near the South Pole, which in turn cools the continental mass of the
East Antarctic ice sheet. The peripheral areas of Antarctica, especially the Antarctic Peninsula, are then subjected to
higher temperatures, which accelerate the melting of the ice. Models suggest that ozone depletion and the enhanced
polar vortex effect may also account for the period of increasing sea ice extent, lasting from when observation started in
the late 1970s until 2014. Since then, the coverage of Antarctic sea ice has decreased rapidly.
Biodiversity
Most species in Antarctica seem to be the descendants of species that lived there millions of years ago. As such, they
must have survived multiple <color=#3366CC>glacial cycles</color>. The species survived the periods of extremely cold climate in isolated
warmer areas, such as those with <color=#3366CC>geothermal heat</color> or areas that remained ice-free throughout the colder climate.
Animals
Invertebrate life of Antarctica includes species of microscopic <color=#3366CC>mites</color> such as Alaskozetes antarcticus, <color=#3366CC>lice</color>, <color=#3366CC>fleas</color>

(Glaciopsyllus antarcticus), <color=#3366CC>nematodes</color>, <color=#3366CC>tardigrades</color>, <color=#3366CC>rotifers</color>, <color=#3366CC>krill</color> and <color=#3366CC>springtails</color>. The flightless <color=#3366CC>midge</color> Belgica
antarctica, the largest purely terrestrial animal in Antarctica, reaches 6 mm in size.
Antarctic krill, which congregates in large <color=#3366CC>schools</color>, is the <color=#3366CC>keystone species</color> of the <color=#3366CC>ecosystem</color> of the Southern Ocean,
being an important food organism for whales, seals, <color=#3366CC>leopard seals</color>, fur seals, <color=#3366CC>squid</color>, icefish, and many bird species,
such as penguins and <color=#3366CC>albatrosses</color>. Some species of marine animals exist and rely, directly or indirectly, on

<color=#3366CC>phytoplankton</color>. Antarctic sea life includes <color=#3366CC>penguins</color>, <color=#3366CC>blue whales</color>, <color=#3366CC>orcas</color>, <color=#3366CC>colossal squids</color> and <color=#3366CC>fur seals</color>. The Antarctic fur
seal was very heavily hunted in the 18th and 19th centuries for its <color=#3366CC>pelt</color> by seal hunters from the United States and the
United Kingdom. Leopard seals are <color=#3366CC>apex predators</color> in the Antarctic ecosystem and migrate across the Southern Ocean
in search of food.
There are approximately 40 bird species that breed on or close to Antarctica, including species of <color=#3366CC>petrels</color>, <color=#3366CC>penguins</color>,
<color=#3366CC>cormorants</color>, and <color=#3366CC>gulls</color>. Various other bird species visit the ocean around Antarctica, including some that normally reside
in the Arctic. The <color=#3366CC>emperor penguin</color> is the only penguin that breeds during the winter in Antarctica; it and the Adélie
penguin breed farther south than any other penguin.
A Census of Marine Life by some 500 researchers during the International Polar Year was released in 2010. The
research found that more than 235 marine organisms live in both polar regions, having bridged the gap of 12000 km.
Large animals such as some <color=#3366CC>cetaceans</color> and birds make the round trip annually. Smaller forms of life, such as <color=#3366CC>sea</color>
<color=#3366CC>cucumbers</color> and free-swimming snails, are also found in both polar oceans. Factors that may aid in their distribution
include temperature differences between the deep ocean at the poles and the equator of no more than 5 C-change and
the major current systems or marine conveyor belts which are able to transport eggs and <color=#3366CC>larva</color>.
In January 2025, the detachment of the massive iceberg A-84 (comparable in size to the city of <color=#3366CC>Chicago</color>) from the
George VI Ice Shelf provided a rare opportunity to explore the seafloor beneath floating ice shelves using robotic
submersibles. Researchers uncovered ecosystems unexpectedly rich in <color=#3366CC>large corals</color>, <color=#3366CC>ancient sponges</color>, <color=#3366CC>icefish</color>, giant
<color=#3366CC>sea spiders</color>, and even <color=#3366CC>octopuses</color> at depths of up to 1300 m. These ecosystems may harbor novel species that have
remained concealed for centuries, sustained by nutrient-bearing ocean currents.
Fungi
About 1,150 species of <color=#3366CC>fungi</color> have been recorded in the Antarctic region, of which about 750 are non-<color=#3366CC>lichen</color>-forming.
Some of the species, having evolved under extreme conditions, have colonised structural cavities within porous rocks
and have contributed to shaping the rock formations of the McMurdo Dry Valleys and surrounding mountain ridges.
The simplified <color=#3366CC>morphology</color> of such fungi, along with their similar biological structures, <color=#3366CC>metabolism systems</color> capable of
remaining active at very low temperatures, and reduced life cycles, make them well suited to such environments. Their
thick-walled and strongly <color=#3366CC>melanised</color> cells make them resistant to <color=#3366CC>UV</color> radiation. An Antarctic <color=#3366CC>endemic</color> species, the
crust-like lichen Buellia frigida, has been used as a <color=#3366CC>model organism</color> in <color=#3366CC>astrobiology</color> research.
The same features can be observed in algae and <color=#3366CC>cyanobacteria</color>, suggesting that they are <color=#3366CC>adaptations</color> to the conditions
prevailing in Antarctica. This has led to speculation that <color=#3366CC>life on Mars</color> might have been similar to Antarctic fungi, such as
Cryomyces antarcticus and Cryomyces minteri. Some of the species of fungi, which are apparently endemic to
Antarctica, live in bird dung, and have evolved so they can grow inside extremely cold dung, but can also pass through
the intestines of warm-blooded animals.
Plants
Throughout its history, Antarctica has seen a wide variety of plant life. In the <color=#3366CC>Cretaceous</color>, it was dominated by a
fern-<color=#3366CC>conifer</color> ecosystem, which changed into a temperate <color=#3366CC>rainforest</color> by the end of that period. During the colder
<color=#3366CC>Neogene</color> (17–2.5 Ma), a <color=#3366CC>tundra</color> ecosystem replaced the rainforests. The climate of present-day Antarctica does not
allow extensive vegetation to form. A combination of freezing temperatures, poor soil quality, and a lack of moisture
and sunlight inhibit plant growth, causing low species diversity and limited distribution. The flora largely consists of

<color=#3366CC>bryophytes</color> (25 species of <color=#3366CC>liverworts</color> and 100 species of <color=#3366CC>mosses</color>). There are three species of <color=#3366CC>flowering plants</color>, all of
which are found in the Antarctic Peninsula: Deschampsia antarctica (Antarctic hair grass), Colobanthus quitensis
(Antarctic pearlwort) and the non-native Poa annua (annual bluegrass).
Other organisms
Of the 700 species of algae in Antarctica, around half are marine <color=#3366CC>phytoplankton</color>. Multicoloured snow algae are
especially abundant in the coastal regions during the summer. Even <color=#3366CC>sea ice</color> can harbour unique ecological
communities, as it expels all salt from the water when it freezes, which accumulates into pockets of <color=#3366CC>brine</color> that also
harbour dormant microorganisms. When the ice begins to melt, brine pockets expand and can combine to form brine
channels, and the <color=#3366CC>algae</color> inside the pockets can reawaken and thrive until the next freeze. Bacteria have also been
found as deep as 800 m under the ice. It is thought to be likely that there exists a native bacterial community within the
subterranean water body of <color=#3366CC>Lake Vostok</color>. The existence of life there is thought to strengthen the argument for the
possibility of life on <color=#3366CC>Jupiter</color>'s moon <color=#3366CC>Europa</color>, which may have water beneath its water-ice crust. There exists a
community of <color=#3366CC>extremophile</color> bacteria in the highly <color=#3366CC>alkaline</color> waters of Lake Untersee. The prevalence of highly resilient
creatures in such inhospitable areas could further bolster the argument for <color=#3366CC>extraterrestrial life</color> in cold, <color=#3366CC>methane</color>-rich
environments.
Conservation and environmental protection
The first international agreement to protect Antarctica's biodiversity was adopted in 1964. The <color=#3366CC>overfishing</color> of <color=#3366CC>krill</color> (an
animal that plays a large role in the Antarctic ecosystem) led officials to enact regulations on fishing. The Convention
for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources, an international treaty that came into force in 1980,
regulates fisheries, aiming to preserve ecological relationships. Despite these regulations, illegal fishing—particularly of
the highly prized Patagonian toothfish which is marketed as Chilean sea bass in the U.S.—remains a problem.
In analogy to the 1980 treaty on sustainable fishing, countries led by New Zealand and the United States negotiated a
treaty on mining. This Convention on the Regulation of Antarctic Mineral Resource Activities was adopted in 1988. After
a strong campaign from environmental organisations, first Australia and then France decided not to ratify the treaty.
Instead, countries adopted the Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty (the Madrid Protocol),
which entered into force in 1998. The Madrid Protocol bans all mining, designating the continent as a "natural reserve
devoted to peace and science".
The pressure group <color=#3366CC>Greenpeace</color> established a base on Ross Island from 1987 to 1992 as part of its attempt to
establish the continent as a World Park. The Southern Ocean Whale Sanctuary was established in 1994 by the
International Whaling Commission. It covers 50 e6km2 and completely surrounds the Antarctic continent. All
<color=#3366CC>commercial whaling</color> is banned in the zone, though Japan has continued to hunt whales in the area, ostensibly for
research purposes.
Despite these protections, the biodiversity in Antarctica is still at risk from human activities. Specially protected areas
cover less than 2% of the area and provide better protection for animals with popular appeal than for less visible
animals. There are more terrestrial protected areas than marine protected areas. Ecosystems are impacted by local
and global threats, notably <color=#3366CC>pollution</color>, the <color=#3366CC>invasion of non-native species</color>, and the various <color=#3366CC>effects of climate change</color>.
History of exploration
Early world maps, like the 1513 Piri Reis map, feature the hypothetical continent Terra Australis. Much larger than and
unrelated to Antarctica, Terra Australis was a landmass that <color=#3366CC>classical</color> scholars presumed necessary to balance the
known lands in the northern hemisphere.
<color=#3366CC>Captain James Cook</color>'s ships, and, crossed the Antarctic Circle on 17 January 1773, in December 1773, and again in
January 1774. Cook came within about 75 mi of the Antarctic coast before retreating in the face of <color=#3366CC>field ice</color> in January
1773. In 1775, he called the existence of a polar continent "probable", and in another copy of his journal he wrote: "[I]
firmly believe it and it's more than probable that we have seen a part of it".
19th century
Sealers were among the earliest to go closer to the Antarctic landmass, perhaps in the earlier part of the 19th century.
The oldest known human remains in the Antarctic region was a skull, dated from 1819 to 1825, that belonged to a
young woman on Yamana Beach at the <color=#3366CC>South Shetland Islands</color>. The woman, who was likely to have been part of a
sealing expedition, was found in 1985.
The first person to see Antarctica or its ice shelf was long thought to have been the British sailor Edward Bransfield, a
captain in the <color=#3366CC>Royal Navy</color>, who discovered the tip of the Antarctic peninsula on 30 January 1820. However, a captain in
the Imperial Russian Navy, <color=#3366CC>Fabian Gottlieb von Bellingshausen</color>, recorded seeing an ice shelf on 27 January. The
American sealer Nathaniel Palmer, whose sealing ship was in the region at this time, may also have been the first to
sight the Antarctic Peninsula.
The First Russian Antarctic Expedition, led by Bellingshausen and Mikhail Lazarev on the 985-ton sloop-of-war Vostok
and the 530-ton support vessel Mirny, reached a point within 32 km of <color=#3366CC>Queen Maud Land</color> and recorded sighting an ice
shelf at, on 27 January 1820. The sighting happened three days before Bransfield sighted the land of the Trinity
Peninsula of Antarctica, as opposed to the ice of an ice shelf, and 10 months before Palmer did so in November 1820.
The first documented landing on Antarctica was by the English-born American sealer John Davis, apparently at Hughes
Bay on 7 February 1821, although some historians dispute this claim, as there is no evidence Davis landed on the
Antarctic continent rather than an offshore island.
On 22 January 1840, two days after the discovery of the coast west of the <color=#3366CC>Balleny Islands</color>, some members of the crew
of the 1837–1840 expedition of the French explorer <color=#3366CC>Jules Dumont d'Urville</color> disembarked on the Dumoulin Islands, off
the coast of Adélie Land, where they took some mineral, algae, and animal samples, erected the French flag, and
claimed French <color=#3366CC>sovereignty over the territory</color>. The American captain Charles Wilkes led an expedition in 1838–1839
and was the first to claim he had discovered the continent. The British naval officer <color=#3366CC>James Clark Ross</color> failed to realise
that what he referred to as "the various patches of land recently discovered by the American, French and English
navigators on the verge of the Antarctic Circle" were connected to form a single continent. The American explorer
Mercator Cooper landed on East Antarctica on 26 January 1853.
The first confirmed landing on the continental mass of Antarctica occurred in 1895 when the Norwegian-Swedish
<color=#3366CC>whaling</color> ship Antarctic reached Cape Adare.
20th century
During the Nimrod Expedition led by the British explorer <color=#3366CC>Ernest Shackleton</color> in 1907, parties led by Edgeworth David
became the first to climb <color=#3366CC>Mount Erebus</color> and to reach the <color=#3366CC>south magnetic pole</color>. Between December 1908 and February
1909, Shackleton and three members of his expedition became the first humans to traverse the <color=#3366CC>Ross Ice Shelf</color>, the first
to cross the Transantarctic Mountains (via the Beardmore Glacier), and the first to set foot on the south Polar Plateau.
On 14 December 1911, <color=#3366CC>an expedition</color> led by Norwegian explorer <color=#3366CC>Roald Amundsen</color> from the ship Fram became the first
to reach the geographic South Pole, using a route from the Bay of Whales and up the Axel Heiberg Glacier. One month
later, the doomed Terra Nova Expedition reached the pole.
The American explorer <color=#3366CC>Richard E. Byrd</color> led four expeditions to Antarctica during the 1920s, 1930s, and 1940s, using
the first mechanised tractors. His expeditions conducted extensive geographical and scientific research, and he is
credited with surveying a larger region of the continent than any other explorer. In 1937, Ingrid Christensen became the
first woman to step onto the Antarctic mainland. Caroline Mikkelsen had landed on an island of Antarctica, earlier in
The South Pole was next reached on 31 October 1956, when a U.S. Navy group led by Rear Admiral George J. Dufek
landed an aircraft there. Six women were flown to the South Pole as a publicity stunt in 1969. In the summer of
1996–1997, Norwegian explorer Børge Ousland became the first person to cross Antarctica alone from coast to coast,
helped by a kite on parts of the journey. Ousland holds the record for the fastest unsupported journey to the South
Pole, taking 34 days.
Demographics
The first semi-permanent inhabitants of regions near Antarctica (areas situated south of the Antarctic Convergence)
were British and American sealers who used to spend a year or more on <color=#3366CC>South Georgia</color>, from 1786 onward. During the
<color=#3366CC>whaling</color> era, which lasted until 1966, the population of the island varied from over 1,000 in the summer (over 2,000 in
some years) to some 200 in the winter. Most of the whalers were Norwegian, with an increasing proportion from Britain.
The first child born in the southern polar region was a Norwegian girl, Solveig Gunbjørg Jacobsen, born in Grytviken on
8 October 1913. Emilio Marcos Palma was the first person born on the Antarctic mainland at the Esperanza Base of the
Argentine Army, on 7 January 1978.
Antarctica's population consists mostly of the staff of research stations in Antarctica (which are continuously maintained
despite the population decline in the winter), although there are 2 all-civilian bases in Antarctica: the Esperanza Base
and the <color=#3366CC>Villa Las Estrellas base</color>. The number of people conducting and supporting scientific research and other work
on the continent and its nearby islands varies from about 1,200 in winter to about 4,800 in the summer, with an
additional 136 people in the winter to 266 people in the summer from the 2 civilian bases (as of 2017). Some of the
research stations are staffed year-round, the winter-over personnel typically arriving from their home countries for a
one-year assignment. <color=#3366CC>Christianity</color> is the most common Antarctic religion, with 8 chapels of various Christian
denominations located there; due to the difficulties involved with transporting religious officials to the continent most
services are performed online. Antarctic English, a distinct variety of the <color=#3366CC>English language</color>, has been found to be
spoken by people living on Antarctica and the subantarctic islands.
Politics
Antarctica's status is regulated by the 1959 <color=#3366CC>Antarctic Treaty</color> and other related agreements, collectively called the
Antarctic Treaty System. Antarctica is defined as all land and ice shelves south of 60° S for the purposes of the Treaty
System. The treaty was signed by twelve countries, including the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color>, the United Kingdom, Argentina, <color=#3366CC>Chile</color>,
Australia, and the United States. Since 1959, a further 42 countries have acceded to the treaty. Countries can
participate in decision-making if they can demonstrate that they do significant research on Antarctica; as of 2022, 29
countries have this 'consultative status'. Decisions are based on consensus, instead of a <color=#3366CC>vote</color>. The treaty set aside
Antarctica as a scientific preserve and established freedom of scientific investigation and environmental protection.
Several countries with research stations in Antarctica allow their citizens stationed in the continent to vote in their
elections.
Territorial claims
In 1539, the King of Spain, <color=#3366CC>Charles V</color>, created the Governorate of Terra Australis, which encompassed lands south of
the <color=#3366CC>Strait of Magellan</color> and thus the then-hypothetical Antarctica, granting this Governorate to Pedro Sancho de la Hoz.
Spain claimed all the territories to the south of the Strait of Magellan until the <color=#3366CC>South Pole</color>, with eastern and western
borders to these claims specified in the <color=#3366CC>Treaty of Tordesillas</color> and <color=#3366CC>Zaragoza</color> respectively. In 1555 the claim was
incorporated to Chile.
In the present, sovereignty over regions of Antarctica is claimed by seven different countries. While a few of these
countries have mutually recognised each other's claims, the validity of the claims is not recognised universally. New
claims on Antarctica have been suspended since 1959, although in 2015, Norway formally defined Queen Maud Land
as including the unclaimed area between it and the South Pole.
The Argentine, British, and Chilean claims overlap and have caused friction. In 2012, after the British Foreign &
Commonwealth Office designated a previously unnamed area Queen Elizabeth Land in tribute to <color=#3366CC>Queen Elizabeth II</color>'s
Diamond Jubilee, the Argentine government protested against the claim. The UK passed some of the areas it claimed
to Australia and New Zealand after they achieved independence. The claims by Britain, Australia, New Zealand,
France, and Norway do not overlap and are recognised by each other. Other member nations of the Antarctic Treaty do
not recognise any claim, yet have shown some form of territorial interest in the past.
• <color=#3366CC>Brazil</color> has a designated "zone of interest" that is not considered an actual claim.
• <color=#3366CC>Peru</color> formally reserved its right to make a claim.
• <color=#3366CC>Russia</color> inherited the Soviet Union's right to claim territory under the original Antarctic Treaty.
• <color=#3366CC>South Africa</color> formally reserved its right to make a claim.
• <color=#3366CC>United States</color> reserved its right to make a claim in the original Antarctic Treaty.
Economy and tourism

Deposits of coal, <color=#3366CC>hydrocarbons</color>, iron ore, <color=#3366CC>platinum</color>, <color=#3366CC>copper</color>, <color=#3366CC>chromium</color>, <color=#3366CC>nickel</color>, <color=#3366CC>gold</color>, and other minerals have been found
in Antarctica, but not in large enough quantities to extract. The Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic
Treaty, which came into effect in 1998 and is due to be reviewed in 2048, restricts the exploitation of Antarctic
resources, including minerals.
<color=#3366CC>Tourists</color> have been visiting Antarctica since 1957. Tourism is subject to the provisions of the Antarctic Treaty and
Environmental Protocol; the self-regulatory body for the industry is the International Association of Antarctica Tour
Operators. Tourists arrive by small or medium ship at specific scenic locations with accessible concentrations of iconic
wildlife. Much Antarctic tourism is based around bird watching tours due to the high numbers of <color=#3366CC>penguins</color> on the
continent. McDonald Beach is known to be a high-traffic area for tourists watching the Adélie penguin population there.
Overland sightseeing flights operated out of Australia and New Zealand until the Mount Erebus disaster in 1979, when
an Air New Zealand plane crashed into Mount Erebus, killing all of the 257 people on board. <color=#3366CC>Qantas</color> resumed
commercial overflights to Antarctica from Australia in the mid-1990s.
Over 74,000 tourists visited the region during the 2019–2020 season, of which 18,500 travelled on cruise ships but did
not leave them to explore on land. Some nature conservation groups have expressed concern over the potential
adverse effects caused by the influx of visitors and have called for limits on the size of visiting <color=#3366CC>cruise ships</color> and a
tourism quota. The primary response by Antarctic Treaty parties has been to develop guidelines that set landing limits
and closed or restricted zones on the more frequently visited sites.
Research
In 2017, there were more than 4,400 scientists undertaking research in Antarctica, a number that fell to just over 1,100
in the winter. There are over 70 permanent and seasonal research stations on the continent; the largest, United States'
<color=#3366CC>McMurdo Station</color>, is capable of housing more than 1,000 people. The British Antarctic Survey has five major research
stations on Antarctica, one of which is completely portable. The Belgian Princess Elisabeth station is one of the most
modern stations and the first to be carbon-neutral. Argentina, Australia, Chile, and Russia also have a large scientific
presence on Antarctica. Many nations release strategy reports designed to guide their research efforts on Antarctica.
The British Antarctic Survey (BAS), Australian Antarctic Program (AAP) and United States Antarctic Program (USAP)
have all released such reports, largely focusing on how changes in Antarctica's climate may impact their respective
home countries and the global climate.

<color=#3366CC>Geologists</color> primarily study <color=#3366CC>plate tectonics</color>, <color=#3366CC>meteorites</color>, and the breakup of Gondwana. <color=#3366CC>Glaciologists</color> study the history
and dynamics of floating ice, seasonal <color=#3366CC>snow</color>, glaciers, and ice sheets. Biologists, in addition to researching wildlife, are
interested in how low temperatures and the presence of humans affect adaptation and survival strategies in organisms.
Biomedical scientists have made discoveries concerning the spreading of <color=#3366CC>viruses</color> and the body's response to extreme
seasonal temperatures.
The view of space from Earth is improved by a thinner atmosphere at higher elevations and a lack of water vapour in
the atmosphere caused by freezing temperatures. <color=#3366CC>Astrophysicists</color> at the <color=#3366CC>Amundsen–Scott South Pole Station</color> study
<color=#3366CC>cosmic microwave background radiation</color> and <color=#3366CC>neutrinos</color> from space. The largest neutrino detector in the world, the
<color=#3366CC>IceCube Neutrino Observatory</color>, is at the Amundsen-Scott Station. It consists of around 5,500 digital optical modules,
some of which reach a depth of 2450 m, that are held in 1 km3 of ice. Scientists also observed higher radiation dose
rates around the coast of Antarctica compared with the global average: this is attributed to cosmic rays going through
the thinner atmosphere compared to equatorial latitudes.
Antarctica provides a unique environment for the study of meteorites: the dry polar desert preserves them well, and
meteorites older than a million years have been found. They are relatively easy to find, as the dark stone meteorites
stand out in a landscape of ice and snow, and the flow of ice accumulates them in certain areas. The Adelie Land
meteorite, discovered in 1912, was the first to be found. Meteorites contain clues about the composition of the <color=#3366CC>Solar</color>
<color=#3366CC>System</color> and its early development. Most meteorites come from asteroids, but a few meteorites found in Antarctica came
from the Moon and Mars.
Culture
Film
The first motion-picture footage of Antarctica is thought to have been hand-cranked by a unknown member of the
Scottish National Antarctic Expedition in early 1904. Film critic William Arnold, writing on the centenary of that event in
2004, cited South (1919), the Oscar-winning With Byrd at the South Pole (1930), 90° South: With Scott to the Antarctic
(1933), The Secret Land (1948), and the IMAX production Edurance: Shackleton's Legendary Antarctic Adventure
(2000) as some of the more notable Antarctic documentaries.
Among the fiction films shot partly or entirely in Antarctica are Mr. Forbush and the Penguins, a 1971 British comedy
starring <color=#3366CC>John Hurt</color>; Antarctica, a 1983 Japanese survival drama with music by <color=#3366CC>Vangelis</color>; and South of Sanity, a 2012
low-budget British <color=#3366CC>horror</color>. The Winter International Film Festival of Antarctica (WIFFA), established in 2006 as a way to
combat social isolation, is held annually for those wintering on the continent. WIFFA is open to <color=#3366CC>short films</color> of 5 minutes
or less, shot during a 48-hour window.
Recreation
The southernmost music festival in the world, Icestock, has been held at McMurdo Station since 1989. The organizers,
performers, and attendees of Icestock are all personnel working at McMurdo or nearby Scott Base.
Sporting events held on Antarctica include the Antarctic Ice Marathon & 100k ultra race, Antarctica Marathon and
Antarctica Cup Yacht Race. Association football has been played since the early twentieth century, with teams
representing bases or visiting ships.
There are two principal holidays celebrated across Antarctica: Midwinter Day on the day of the southern <color=#3366CC>winter solstice</color>
(June 20 or 21) and Antarctica Day on December 1, which commemorates the signing of the Antarctic Treaty in 1959.
Halloween
Halloween, also known as All Hallows' Eve, or All Saints' Eve, is a celebration observed in many countries on 31
October, the eve of the Western Christian feast of All Hallows' Day. It is at the beginning of the observance of
Allhallowtide, the time in the Christian <color=#3366CC>liturgical year</color> dedicated to remembering the dead, including <color=#3366CC>saints</color> (<color=#3366CC>hallows</color>),
martyrs, and all the faithful departed. In popular culture, Halloween has become a celebration of <color=#3366CC>horror</color> and is
associated with the macabre and the <color=#3366CC>supernatural</color>.
One theory holds that many Halloween traditions were influenced by <color=#3366CC>Celtic</color> <color=#3366CC>harvest festivals</color>, particularly the Gaelic
festival <color=#3366CC>Samhain</color>, which are believed to have <color=#3366CC>pagan</color> roots. Some theories go further and suggest that Samhain may
have been Christianized as All Hallows' Day, along with its eve, by the Church. Other academics say Halloween began
independently as a <color=#3366CC>Christian</color> holiday, being the vigil of All Hallows' Day. Celebrated in <color=#3366CC>Ireland</color> and <color=#3366CC>Scotland</color> for
centuries, <color=#3366CC>Irish</color> and Scottish immigrants brought many Halloween customs to North America in the 19th century, and
then through American influence various Halloween customs spread to other countries by the late 20th and early 21st
centuries.
Popular activities during Halloween include <color=#3366CC>trick-or-treating</color> (or the related <color=#3366CC>guising</color> and souling), attending Halloween
costume parties, carving pumpkins or turnips into <color=#3366CC>jack-o'-lanterns</color>, lighting <color=#3366CC>bonfires</color>, apple bobbing, <color=#3366CC>divination</color> games,
playing <color=#3366CC>pranks</color>, visiting haunted attractions, telling frightening stories, and watching horror or Halloween-themed films.
Some Christians practice the observances of All Hallows' Eve, including attending <color=#3366CC>church services</color> and lighting candles
on the graves of the dead, although it is a secular celebration for others. Historically, some Christians abstained from
meat on All Hallows' Eve, a tradition reflected in the eating of certain vegetarian foods on this day, including apples,
potato pancakes, and soul cakes.
Etymology
Hallow derives from <color=#3366CC>Middle English</color> halowen, from <color=#3366CC>Old English</color> hālig meaning <color=#3366CC>holy</color> and has been used synonymously
with the word <color=#3366CC>saint</color>. The word Halloween or Hallowe'en comes from the <color=#3366CC>Lowland Scots</color> form of All Hallows' Eve (the
evening before All Hallows' Day): even is the Scots term for 'eve' or 'evening', and is contracted to e'en or een; so (All)
Hallow(s) E(v)en became Halloween. A term equivalent to 'All Hallows Eve' as attested in Old English. Thus, the name
has an origin in <color=#3366CC>Christianity</color>, and means 'Saints' eve(ning)'.
History
Christian origins and historical customs
Halloween is influenced by Christian beliefs and practices surrounding All Hallows' Day (All Saints' Day). The English
word 'Halloween' comes from "All Hallows' Eve", being the evening before the Christian holy days of All Hallows' Day
(All Saints' Day) on 1 November and All Souls' Day on 2 November. Since the time of the early Church, major feasts in
Christianity (such as <color=#3366CC>Christmas</color>, <color=#3366CC>Easter</color> and <color=#3366CC>Pentecost</color>) had vigils that began the night before, as did the feast of All
Hallows. These three days are included in the liturgical period of Allhallowtide, a time when Western Christians honour
all Christian martyrs and <color=#3366CC>saints</color>, as well as <color=#3366CC>pray</color> for departed souls.
After the persecution of Christians in the Roman Empire, "there were more martyrs than there were days in the year,
and so one day was set apart in honor of them all, and called All Saints' Day." Commemorations of all saints and
martyrs were held by several churches on various dates, mostly in springtime. In 4th-century Roman Edessa it was
held on 13 May, and on that date in 609, Pope Boniface IV re-dedicated the <color=#3366CC>Pantheon</color> in Rome to "St Mary and all
martyrs". This was the date of Lemuria, an <color=#3366CC>ancient Roman</color> festival of the dead, when it was believed that restless and
vengeful souls wandered. Some folklorists also suggest the ancient Roman festival of Parentalia (including Feralia)
influenced All Saints' and All Souls' days. Parentalia involved a commemorative meal at the graves of relatives, during
which food and drink were offered to the dead, and Christian Romans continued this custom, extending it to the saints
and martyrs.
There is evidence that by 800, churches in Ireland and <color=#3366CC>Northumbria</color> were holding a feast commemorating all saints on
1 November. In 835, the <color=#3366CC>Frankish Empire</color> officially adopted 1 November as the date of All Saints' Day. This may have
been promoted by <color=#3366CC>Alcuin</color> of Northumbria, who was a member of <color=#3366CC>Charlemagne</color>'s court, or by the Irish clerics and
scholars who were also members of the Frankish court. Some suggest the date was due to Celtic influence; others, that
it was a Germanic idea, although it is said that both Germanic- and Celtic-speaking peoples commemorated the dead
at the beginning of winter. They may have seen it as the most fitting time to do so, as it is a time of "dying" in nature. It
is also suggested the change was made on the "practical grounds that Rome in summer could not accommodate the
great number of pilgrims who flocked to it", and perhaps because of <color=#3366CC>public health</color> concerns over <color=#3366CC>Roman Fever</color>, which
claimed a number of lives during Rome's sultry summers.
All Souls' Day, a feast commemorating all deceased Christians, became widespread in the 12th century. Its date was
fixed on 2 November, the day after All Saints' Day. By the end of the 12th century, they had become holy days of
obligation requiring church attendance in Western Christianity and involved such traditions as ringing church bells for
souls in <color=#3366CC>Purgatory</color>. It was also "customary for criers dressed in black to parade the streets, ringing a bell of mournful
sound and calling on all good Christians to remember the poor souls".
The Allhallowtide custom of baking and sharing soul cakes for all <color=#3366CC>christened</color> souls has been suggested as the origin of
trick-or-treating. The custom dates back at least as far as the 15th century and was found in parts of England, Wales,
Flanders, Bavaria and Austria. Groups of poor people, often children, would go door to door during Allhallowtide,
